items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Councillor Freeman opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

I offer this acknowledgement with respect and gratitude, recognizing that my life has unfolded across lands governed by longstanding treaty relationships between Indigenous Nations and the Crown. These treaties—historic, living, and often unfulfilled—shape the places that have sustained me and continue to guide my understanding of responsibility and reconciliation.
My life began in Toronto, on lands covered by Treaty 13, the Toronto Purchase of 1805, made with the Mississaugas of the Credit.

I was raised in Woodstock, Ontario, within the territory governed by the Upper Canada Treaties, specifically Treaty 3, the Between the Lakes Purchase of 1792. These agreements involve the Haudenosaunee, Anishinaabeg, and Neutral (Attiwonderonk) Peoples.

As I moved to Waterloo for university and early career opportunities, I lived and worked within the lands encompassed by the Haldimand Tract, granted to the Six Nations in 1784 – six miles on either side of the Grand River. This region also falls within the Between the Lakes Treaty territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit.

During my time as President of Professional Engineers Ontario, I travelled across many treaty territories throughout Canada. These journeys deepened my awareness of the diversity of treaty histories and the responsibilities they carry, and how these agreements continue to shape the identities and governance of the provinces and territories.

Since August of last year, I have been privileged to temporarily live and work in the Northwest Territories, on lands governed by Treaty 8 and Treaty 11, within the traditional territories of the Yellowknives Dene First Nation (Drygeese Territory) and the North Slave Métis.

In preparing for engineering work at Ipperwash recently, I undertook a two-day awareness program to learn about the history of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, whose lands are shaped by complex and painful treaty relationships, including the legacy of Treaty 29 and the broader Upper Canada Treaties. Through this learning, I was reminded of the Seven Grandfather Teachings, which continue to influence how I understand my responsibilities within treaty relationships.

Across each stage of my life, these treaties remind me that I am a guest on lands whose histories long predate my own. I acknowledge these treaty relationships as ongoing commitments – ones that call for learning, respect, and meaningful action.

items.title: Notice of Motion
notes: Councillor Bodaly – Bill 60 Motion
Motion to be tabled June 15, 2026 for Council consideration June 22, 2026.
Motion:
WHEREAS the Province of Ontario’s Bill 60, Fighting Delays, Building Faster Act, 2025 was passed in November of 2025; and
WHEREAS Schedule 16 of Bill 60 enacts the Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025; and
WHEREAS the Act allows the Province to designate water corporations to manage water and wastewater services; and

WHEREAS the Province has now enacted legislative amendments through Bill 98 to reinforce 100 per cent public sector ownership of water and wastewater public corporations, which reflects an important step in addressing concerns regarding ownership structures; and while the City recognizes this commitment, it remains important that the implementation of any such model continues to support strong municipal oversight, transparency, accountability, rate setting authority, asset stewardship, and long term integrated planning; and
WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo has a lengthy history of managing our water and wastewater system, governed within a robust regulatory framework; and

WHEREAS the current water capacity challenges within the Region of Waterloo underscore how foundational water security is to growth management, housing, economic stability and climate resilience within the Region; and
WHEREAS Regional decision making, rate setting and governance are transparently governed by open meeting rules, allowing for complete public engagement; and
WHEREAS the City of Waterloo is ultimately responsible for the local distribution and delivery of water to end users.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Waterloo affirms its support for the continued public ownership and governance of drinking water and wastewater services, recognizing water as essential to public health, environmental protection, and long-term community well-being; and BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Waterloo encourages the Province of Ontario to review Schedule 16 of Bill 60 through a lens of public health and system resilience, groundwater protection and long-term water security, governance, accountability, and transparency financial sustainability, and affordability, planning, growth management, and climate adaptation; and BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Waterloo encourages the Province of Ontario to enact and maintain explicit statutory protections requiring public-sector ownership of water and wastewater corporations, including prohibitions on private share ownership or transfer; and BE IT RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution be sent to the Premier of Ontario, the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, to local and area MPP’s, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, the Ontario Big City Mayors, and to the Region of Waterloo and local area municipalities.

items.title: Questions
notes: Councillor Hanmer had a question of staff regarding the communications surrounding the Informal Public Meeting next week, and what else the City can do to inform the public, especially where the notices haven’t been delivered. Commissioner Ron Ormson responded that the Informal Public Meeting could be deferred, if Council requested it, and that they use multiple methods of delivery to try to ensure the public is aware. Cari Van Niekerk added that the City could post small signs at the locations and put out additional correspondence.

items.title: New Business
notes: Councillor Wright mentioned that yesterday, June 14, was the Grand Porch Party in the Uptown West Neighbourhood. Despite the heavy rain, there were many people out to enjoy the music hosted on front porches. She gave a shoutout to the community volunteers who make this festival possible, as it draws people from all across Uptown.

Councillor Wright also highlighted that on this upcoming Saturday, June 20, there will be an Indigenous Market in the Waterloo Town Square to coincide with Indigenous History Month. There will be more than 20 Indigenous vendors and live music Mayor McCabe noted that on Saturday evening, June 13, she attended a dinner and awards ceremony for the Kitchener-Waterloo Philatelic Society, which was hosting The Royal Philatelic Society of Canada exhibition from June 12-14 at the Waterloo Memorial Recreation Complex. People came from across North America for the stamp collecting display, and had great things to say about the staff for their help.

Councillor Freeman mentioned that Saturday is a busy day, especially with school wrapping up. Many army cadets are having their ceremonial reviews throughout the Region, including the Waterloo Cadets Corp at Albert McCormick Community Centre.
Councillor Freeman also noted that the Eastbridge Neighbourhood Association is hosting their annual food truck festival in Eastbridge Park, and hopes the weather is good for everyone’s events.

motions.text: 1. That Council approve report CORP2026-034. 2. That Council approves a 30% reduction in-principle to all residential Development Charge categories, retroactive to March 30, 2026, for a three-year period, as required to qualify for the DCRP program with the implementation of the DC reduction being subject to the City being approved for DCRP grant funding. 3. That Council directs staff to take the necessary steps to extend the Residential Development Charge rate relief approved to eligible residential DC permits issued on or after March 30, 2026, when the program was first announced subject to the City being approved for DCRP grant funding. 4. That Council acknowledge that as part of the DCRP program, current residential DCs will be frozen at the 30% reduced rates for a period of three-years and annual indexing of Residential Development Charges on December 1, 2026, December 1, 2027, December 1, 2028, in accordance with the second quarter Statistics Canada Non-residential Building Construction Price Index for Toronto in accordance with section 5(1) of the Development Charges Act will temporarily not be permitted. 5. That Council directs staff to prepare an application to the Development Charge Reduction Program in support of the Conservation Drive Sanitary Pumping Station project identified in the City’s current approved capital forecast (ref #590) and Development Charge By-law (DC-051) in the amount of $11,500,000 with the Federal and Provincial governments providing up to 90% of the eligible project cost, supporting the addition of 2,000 housing units. 6. That Council approve funding in the amount of up to $1,150,000 funded from the Sanitary Sewer Utility Capital Reserve for the City’s 10% share of the Conservation Drive Sanitary Pumping Station project. 7. That Council directs staff to prepare an application to the Development Charge Reduction Program in support of the Erbsville Road - Ira Needles to Columbia St – Watermain Expansion project identified in the City’s current approved capital forecast (ref #610) and Development Charge By-law (DC-056) in the amount of $4,934,000 with the Federal and Provincial governments providing up to 90% of the eligible project cost, supporting the addition of 850 housing units. 8. That Council approve funding in the amount of up to $493,400 funded from the Water Utility Capital Reserve for the City’s 10% share of the Erbsville Road - Ira Needles to Columbia St – Watermain Expansion project. 9. That Council direct staff to start construction of the Conservation Drive Sanitary Pumping Station project and the Erbsville Road - Ira Needles to Columbia St – Watermain Expansion project on or before July 31, 2030, and complete the project by October 31, 2035, or sooner as required under the DCRP, subject to the City being approved for DCRP grant funding. 10. That should the City’s Ontario and Canada Development Charge Reduction Grant application be successful in full or substantially in part, Council authorize the Mayor and Clerk to sign the grant transfer payment agreement(s) and any other related documents subject to the satisfaction of the City Solicitor.
motions.text_html:
1. That Council approve report CORP2026-034.

2. That Council approves a 30% reduction in-principle to all residential Development Charge categories, retroactive to March 30, 2026, for a three-year period, as required to qualify for the DCRP program with the implementation of the DC reduction being subject to the City being approved for DCRP grant funding.

3. That Council directs staff to take the necessary steps to extend the Residential Development Charge rate relief approved to eligible residential DC permits issued on or after March 30, 2026, when the program was first announced subject to the City being approved for DCRP grant funding.

4. That Council acknowledge that as part of the DCRP program, current residential DCs will be frozen at the 30% reduced rates for a period of three-years and annual indexing of Residential Development Charges on December 1, 2026, December 1, 2027, December 1, 2028, in accordance with the second quarter Statistics Canada Non-residential Building Construction Price Index for Toronto in accordance with section 5(1) of the Development Charges Act will temporarily not be permitted.

5. That Council directs staff to prepare an application to the Development Charge Reduction Program in support of the Conservation Drive Sanitary Pumping Station project identified in the City’s current approved capital forecast (ref #590) and Development Charge By-law (DC-051) in the amount of $11,500,000 with the Federal and Provincial governments providing up to 90% of the eligible project cost, supporting the addition of 2,000 housing units.

6. That Council approve funding in the amount of up to $1,150,000 funded from the Sanitary Sewer Utility Capital Reserve for the City’s 10% share of the Conservation Drive Sanitary Pumping Station project.

7. That Council directs staff to prepare an application to the Development Charge Reduction Program in support of the Erbsville Road - Ira Needles to Columbia St – Watermain Expansion project identified in the City’s current approved capital forecast (ref #610) and Development Charge By-law (DC-056) in the amount of $4,934,000 with the Federal and Provincial governments providing up to 90% of the eligible project cost, supporting the addition of 850 housing units.

8. That Council approve funding in the amount of up to $493,400 funded from the Water Utility Capital Reserve for the City’s 10% share of the Erbsville Road - Ira Needles to Columbia St – Watermain Expansion project.

9. That Council direct staff to start construction of the Conservation Drive Sanitary Pumping Station project and the Erbsville Road - Ira Needles to Columbia St – Watermain Expansion project on or before July 31, 2030, and complete the project by October 31, 2035, or sooner as required under the DCRP, subject to the City being approved for DCRP grant funding.

10. That should the City’s Ontario and Canada Development Charge Reduction Grant application be successful in full or substantially in part, Council authorize the Mayor and Clerk to sign the grant transfer payment agreement(s) and any other related documents subject to the satisfaction of the City Solicitor.
